body:
Review from codex sol xhigh:

```
  ### [P1] Keep materialized scalar caches out of layout selection

  ChunkCursor::new uses lazy_as_materialized_series, which returns the cached Series after a ScalarColumn has been materialized. The scalar can then
  incorrectly become the frame’s layout source.

  This occurs in existing writer code: chunk_df_for_writing materializes the first column while inspecting chunk lengths. For a scalar-first frame whose
  next column has two chunks, chunk_df_for_writing(&mut df, 2) panics in iter_chunks_physical. Release builds subsequently panic in RecordBatch::new
  because the scalar reports the full height while the selected Series chunk is shorter. This affects the Parquet and IPC-stream writers.

  I reproduced this against commit 9348ede993; the identical program succeeds on parent 69a1f9ab4c. The new alignment logic, cursor, and iterator
  dispatch should match Column::Series/use as_series(), ensuring a scalar’s cache never defines its conceptual layout. A scalar-first writer regression
  test would cover this.


```

reviewed from the issue side (#29542 author). the fix matches the root cause we diagnosed there: removing the pre-lowercase pass and casing the original characters directly

i checked the remaining edge cases i could construct against python, all matching:

- decomposed input `'i̇stanbul'` (i + U+0307) → `'İ̇Stanbul'` on both sides. python also capitalizes after the combining mark since it is not cased, so the `!c.is_alphabetic()` boundary rule agrees with `str.title` here
- `'aİb'` → `'Ai̇b'` (İ lowercases to i + U+0307 mid-word)
- `'ẞ foo'` → `'ẞ Foo'` and `'ﬀ foo'` → `'Ff Foo'` (these are the ones that distinguish titlecase mappings from upper mappings)
- `'中文 test'` → `'中文 Test'` (alphabetic uncased chars pass through)

one non-blocking suggestion: adding those cases to the test list would pin exactly the behaviors that broke before, especially the decomposed-input and ligature ones. the python-parity assert style already makes them one-liners

body:
Very exciting! I've been working on and off around this topic since August and have some infos that may be interesting or not:

- I think this PR uses pyarrow compute expressions for predicate pushdown: Unfortunately only a tiny set of predicates can be pushed down to Lance using this route, which I investigated a whole ago here: https://github.com/jonasdedden/polars-pylance/blob/80b61818f10bae9f7c7ff40de702794b895fd202/bench/plots/static/pushdown-coverage.png (Note that in current `polars-pylance`, a few more things are lowerable through the Lance SQL translation, such as `xor`, `str.contains_any`, floor division, `dt.weekday`).
- The limitation here is because of three things: 1. (most important) Not a whole lot of predicates can be expressed as pyarrow compute expressions in general, 2. For a few expressions that *could* be expressible, polars doesn't signal that (examples being [this](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/28996) which is now fixed), 3. Lance's scanner doesn't necessarily use or is compatible with all expressions
  - I've been working on this and fixing a bunch of things upstream, but this hasn't been extremely fruitful, at least for me
  - => The current route in `polars-pylance` is that I instead take in the raw polars expressions and then do a custom polars expressions -> Lance SQL translation, which is vastly more powerful. It comes with the big cost of a lot of added complexity though, as seen here: https://github.com/jonasdedden/polars-pylance/blob/main/src/polars_pylance/_predicate.py
- A lot of the added complexity of the chosen path above  though is due to inconsistencies of niche polars behavior compared to Lance SQL, and Lance and/or Datafusion currently still doing things slightly incorrectly, which I'm also working on consistently to fix upstream. I gathered inconsistencies with corresponding simplifications once solved  so far here: https://github.com/jonasdedden/polars-pylance/blob/73c3c2b8c98f7b6fe222ef9d2d60a1021ba5c3c9/docs/UPSTREAM.md

If you have any questions or other suggestions, please let me know! :) Very happy to discuss this topic, and would be nice to have native Lance integration to polars!

body:
> Can you ask if it does anything with the code generation time? Or the amount of code expanded? It says, no effect -
claude

Good question — let me measure rather than guess.

My work got committed onto a branch by external tooling mid-measurement, so let me first confirm nothing was lost, then measure in isolation.

Refactor intact (commit 8d87a18, exactly my 115 files). Now the measurement — I'll use a synthetic pair since the earlier stash-based baseline got clobbered by that external commit:

Measured rather than assumed. Synthetic crate with 100 call sites of a 10-line body, both macro styles, same nightly as the repo pins:

  | old (\|$T\|) | new (\|T\|) -- | -- | -- body copies per call site | 10 (one per arm) | 10 (one per arm) expanded text (1 call site) | 5,648 B / 544 tok | 6,802 B / 583 tok frontend (--emit=metadata), best of 5 | 0.27 s | 0.27 s full -O build, best of 3 | 1.52 s | 1.52 s object code | 10,056 B | 10,056 B (IR identical modulo symbol names) crate metadata | 314,665 B | 241,498 B

Codegen: unaffected. A type alias is resolved during name resolution and erased before MIR, so each arm monomorphizes exactly as before — optimized LLVM IR diffs only in the crate-name-derived symbol names, and object size is identical to the byte.

Expansion volume: a wash. Both forms duplicate the body once per arm — that was already the cost and it hasn't changed. The new form adds one #[allow(dead_code)] type T = i8; item per arm (~9 tokens), and drops the per-call-site macro_rules! __with_ty__ definition, which itself held an extra copy of the body tokens in the AST. Net expanded text is a few percent larger on a tiny body, proportionally less on the 20–40 line bodies that actually use these macros.

Compile time: no measurable difference at 100 call sites (the repo has 228 in total). The one real shift is metadata: 23% smaller, because the old form created an extra macro definition plus one extra expansion context per arm per call site, and that hygiene/span bookkeeping gets serialized.

Genuine semantic constraints (not style):

  • The metavariable is now a type, not a token, so it only works in type position — that's what forced the pow.rs rewrite (it was being used as a method name, base.i32()), and it would break stringify!($T)-style uses.
  • It shadows a same-named generic in scope instead of being distinct from it — two sites needed the metavar renamed (float_sorted_arg_max.rs → F, asof/groups.rs → B).
  • Arms must bind concrete types; a type item in a block can't reference the enclosing fn's generics. True of all current arms, but it constrains future ones.
  • with_match_pl_num_arith! now binds one let op = … value, so the body gets a single inferred instantiation; the old token substitution would have allowed using it at two different generic types in one body. No call site does.
  • Lints and rustfmt now reach the bodies, which is where those 60 findings came from.

One thing to flag: partway through this, external tooling committed the refactor onto branch nxs/$ as 8d87a18 (diff is exactly my 115 files, 1068/1002). That clobbered a git stash I was using for the before/after baseline on the real crate, which is why the numbers above are synthetic — I verified the work itself is intact.

The one real shift is metadata: 23% smaller, because the old form created an extra macro definition plus one extra expansion context per arm per call site, and that hygiene/span bookkeeping gets serialized. **Genuine semantic constraints** (not style): - The metavariable is now a *type*, not a token, so it only works in type position — that's what forced the [[pow.rs](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/crates/polars-expr/src/dispatch/pow.rs:122)](crates/polars-expr/src/dispatch/pow.rs:122) rewrite (it was being used as a method name, `base.i32()`), and it would break `stringify!($T)`-style uses. - It shadows a same-named generic in scope instead of being distinct from it — two sites needed the metavar renamed ([[float_sorted_arg_max.rs](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/crates/polars-core/src/chunked_array/ops/float_sorted_arg_max.rs:49)](crates/polars-core/src/chunked_array/ops/float_sorted_arg_max.rs:49) → `F`, [[asof/groups.rs](https://claude.ai/epitaxy/crates/polars-ops/src/frame/join/asof/groups.rs:255)](crates/polars-ops/src/frame/join/asof/groups.rs:255) → `B`). - Arms must bind concrete types; a `type` item in a block can't reference the enclosing fn's generics. True of all current arms, but it constrains future ones. - `with_match_pl_num_arith!` now binds one `let op = …` value, so the body gets a single inferred instantiation; the old token substitution would have allowed using it at two different generic types in one body. No call site does. - Lints and rustfmt now reach the bodies, which is where those 60 findings came from. One thing to flag: partway through this, external tooling committed the refactor onto branch `nxs/$` as `8d87a18` (diff is exactly my 115 files, 1068/1002). That clobbered a `git stash` I was using for the before/after baseline on the real crate, which is why the numbers above are synthetic — I verified the work itself is intact.

body:
hi @orlp. The formula is simply `ls / lc < rs / rc`, cross multiplied. lc and rc aren’t cardinalities though. `estimate_cardinality `returns `sketch.estimate() / rows`, which are distinct keys per row. the current `lc * ls < rc * rs` isn’t “cardinality times size per row” either, it’s a ratio times bytes per row and it only means total size if u assume both sides have the same row count. This is rarely true on a join. 

This PR compares ls/lc against rs/rc. It assumes both sides cover the same keys. 

lineitem vs orders at SF30: 0.23 vs 1.0 in the sample, 180M vs 45M rows. current rule builds lineitem.

As for this 

> repeated rows take up less space in our hash table

The keys dedupe, but the payload does not. peak memory for lineitem join orders is 8.6 GiB building lineitem vs 3.8 GiB building orders.

As for writing a benchmark that breaks it, i did. 20M rows per side, one side with 10 keys and the other unique:

| Build | Time | Peak Memory |
|---|---:|---:|
| 10 key side (current) | 2837 ms | 1.55 GiB |
| Unique side (this PR) | 896 ms | 1.94 GiB |

25% more memory but 3x faster, the 10 key build only finalizes on 10 partitions. both rules are guessing once both sides saturate, main just guesses wrong on fact/dim.

body:
hello @ritchie46. I implemented your patch, but there are a few things to note. 

`supertype.rs:483` matches `(Decimal(_, _), Float32 | Float64 | Unknown(UnknownKind::Float))` and returns `Float64`, which shadows the dynamic-literal arm. Dropping `Unknown(UnknownKind::Float)` from it lets the upcast fire.

this does preserve the speed and applies to all operators. However, it does change results for literals that are representable at the column scale. Look at this here: 

 ```
v == 5.555  ->  [5.56]              expected []
v >  5.555  ->  [5.60, 6.00]        expected [5.56, 5.60, 6.00]
v <= 5.555  ->  [5.00, 5.50, 5.56]  expected [5.00, 5.50]
```

The supertype layer can't guard against it: `UnknownKind::Int(i128)` carries its value, but `UnknownKind::Float` doesn't, so there's no way to distinguish 0.05 from 0.055 there, and it’s why this PR sits only in coerce_comparison_literal where the scalar is available. 

So what do u think? We can give `unknownkind::Float` a value so the upcast can check representability, or we could keep this version. let me know which one is optimal

body:
@orlp 

Okay, so I checked and the same thing was happening for subtraction and multiplication. So, I added the same arm to `Operator::Minus` and the catch-all, which handles multiplication, in `get_arithmetic_field`. I updated the test to cover these as well. For division, it was fixed in https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/29122.

However, when running tests, I noticed that the planner and engine disagree on floor division (`//`) and remainder (`%`). The **engine** rejects the `Decimal` dtype entirely:

```bash
python -c "
import polars as pl
pl.DataFrame({'d': [1]}).cast(pl.Decimal(18, 4)).select(pl.col('d') // 1)"

polars.exceptions.InvalidOperationError: floor_div operation not supported for dtype `decimal[18,4]`
This error occurred in the following expression:
        [(col("d").cast(Decimal(38, 4))) // (1.0000)]
```

and 

```bash
python -c "
import polars as pl
pl.DataFrame({'d': [1]}).cast(pl.Decimal(18, 4)).select(pl.col('d') % 1)"

polars.exceptions.InvalidOperationError: `remainder` operation not supported for dtype `decimal[18,4]`
This error occurred in the following expression:
        [(col("d").cast(Decimal(38, 4))) % (1.0000)]
```

But the **planner** still predicts a `Decimal` dtype instead of erroring at `collect_schema()`. Since those route through the same `_` branch as multiplication, they'll now report `Decimal(38, 4)` rather than `Decimal(18, 4)`. This is still wrong since the engine rejects the computation entirely, but it doesn't make it actively worse. 

The proper fix, I believe, is for the planner to reject them up front since the precedent is for the planner to match the engine. It could also be that polars wants to support the `Decimal` dtype in floor division and remainder.

**Questions for you:** Should the planner reject floor division and remainder for `Decimal` dtypes or should the engine support it? Also, would you like this done in this PR or a follow-up PR?

Thanks!

So negating `!null_extend` to `null_extend` here appears to fix everything, but I think we may need @ritchie46 to help us here what the original intent was.

4. If we pass a length 2 df with a length 3 df, and `strict=True`, we raise correctly.

body:
One thing to consider is how strongly do we feel about maintaining the existing behavior, even as an option. If we want to make a breaking change, we can simple match the interface of numpy interp exactly. In other words, you can pass “left” and “right” (not that I love THOSE parameter names) and it will use those as the fill values above and below the range. If they are null, it will use fp[0] and fp[-1]. So there is no way to end up with your existing behavior in that scenario.

I would lean this way personally. When I reach for interpolation, it’s generally because I have some null values and I want to end up with no null values. That can be accomplished with different levels of complexity and fanciness… but the goal is always “get rid of the missing values” so the existing polars behavior means I’m not done. If I don’t like linear interpolation with values above the range filled in with a scalar… well… then maybe I should reach for a more complicated science package outside of polars. “Simple linear interpolation in polars in the range, and then something custom above/below the range” doesn’t seem like all that common of a workflow.

Thanks for the quick reply. Indeed, if we only join two base tables it doesn't make sense to join on the same key columns. body:
> What happens if one of the new dummy columns has the same name as the original column?

That would have to be very contrived. The dummy columns are named by `[original_name]_[value]`. One would have to have explicitly already had a column with that name, and that issue is present on the existing implementation anyway:

```python
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({
    "a": [1, 2, 3],
    "a_1": [1, 2, 3],
})
df.to_dummies("a")
```
```
polars.exceptions.DuplicateError: unable to hstack, column with name "a_1" already exists
```
My guess is that one can contrive many scenarios to collide with polars' renaming, but it's not in our best interest to fight those edge cases.

body:
Hi @MarcoGorelli, I'm interested but I think this is pushing the limits of my polars/rust knowledge.

For example, I'm a bit confused by `broadcast_try_binary_elementwise` and how to handle series of different lengths.
```python
>>> import polars as pl
>>> from datetime import datetime, timedelta
>>>
>>> df = pl.DataFrame(
...     {
...         "datetime": datetime(2000, 2, 3, 12, 30),
...         "every":  ["1y", "1mo", "1d", "1h"],
...         "duration": [timedelta(i) for i in range(4)],
...     }
... )
>>> df
shape: (4, 3)
┌─────────────────────┬───────┬──────────────┐
│ datetime            ┆ every ┆ duration     │
│ ---                 ┆ ---   ┆ ---          │
│ datetime[μs]        ┆ str   ┆ duration[μs] │
╞═════════════════════╪═══════╪══════════════╡
│ 2000-02-03 12:30:00 ┆ 1y    ┆ 0µs          │
│ 2000-02-03 12:30:00 ┆ 1mo   ┆ 1d           │
│ 2000-02-03 12:30:00 ┆ 1d    ┆ 2d           │
│ 2000-02-03 12:30:00 ┆ 1h    ┆ 3d           │
└─────────────────────┴───────┴──────────────┘
```

If I filter "datetime" to a single value but leave all four values of "every", then truncation broadcasts and returns four values:
```python
>>> df.select(
...     pl.col("datetime").filter(pl.col("every") == "1mo")
...         .dt.truncate(pl.col("every"))
... )
shape: (4, 1)
┌─────────────────────┐
│ datetime            │
│ ---                 │
│ datetime[μs]        │
╞═════════════════════╡
│ 2000-01-01 00:00:00 │
│ 2000-02-01 00:00:00 │
│ 2000-02-03 00:00:00 │
│ 2000-02-03 12:00:00 │
└─────────────────────┘
```

If I filter "datetime" to *two values*, then truncation picks the first two of "every" and gives me two values back:
```python
>>> df.select(
...     pl.col("datetime").filter(pl.col("every").is_in(["1mo", "1d"]))
...         .dt.truncate(pl.col("every"))
... )
shape: (2, 1)
┌─────────────────────┐
│ datetime            │
│ ---                 │
│ datetime[μs]        │
╞═════════════════════╡
│ 2000-01-01 00:00:00 │
│ 2000-02-01 00:00:00 │
└─────────────────────┘
```

But if I try other operations that use two series, like addition, I would get an error.
```python
>>> df.select(
...     pl.col("datetime").filter(pl.col("every").is_in(["1mo", "1d"]))
...         + pl.col("duration")
... )
[...]
polars.exceptions.ComputeError: cannot evaluate two Series of different lengths (2 and 4)
[...]
```

Is this the intended behavior?
pr_title: feat: Implement `round` and `truncate` for Duration columns

body:
I think these functions are far too specific in their current form. I think there are multiple use-cases one could have:

1. Find the first/last non-null value. As I [mentioned here](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/22547) I'm open to adding an `ignore_nulls` parameter to `first` and `last`, as this is a really common use-case. Currently you have to write `pl.col.x.filter(pl.col.x.is_not_null()).first()` and similarly for last, which isn't as efficient. Once this exist we can also add an optimization pass for this.

2. Find the index of the first/last non-null value. I think this should not have a dedicated function for nulls but instead be a function on arbitrary boolean masks as it's much less common and in general we would like to push users away from index-based solutions (as they're not streaming friendly).

So, generalizing to arbitrary boolean masks, we have the same two questions again:

1. Find the first/last value using an arbitrary boolean mask. Currently this has to be written `pl.col.x.filter(cond).first()` and `pl.col.x.filter(cond).last()`. I'm not strongly opposed to `Expr.first_where` and `Expr.last_where` which take a boolean mask of equal length to its first and selects the first/last value, with an optimization past to turn `filter().first()`/`filter().last()` into this.

2. Find the index of the first/last true value in an arbitrary boolean mask. We already have an efficient invocation this for the first, namely `.index_of(True)`, but not for the last true value. I would be open to adding a default keyword-only argument `index_of(val, *, last = False)` which when specified to be `True` gives the index of the last matching element. Then we could add an optimization pass which turns `pl.col.x.arg_true().first()` and `pl.col.x.arg_true().last()` into `index_of` calls.
pr_title: feat: Add `index_of_first_not_null` and `index_of_last_not_null` Expr and Series methods

body:
>  I think this should not have a dedicated function for nulls but instead be a function on arbitrary boolean masks as it's much less common

Looking at the large amount of Pandas code we are hoping to translate, I can assure you that it is actually quite common, hence needing some equivalent/clear functionality on our (Polars) side.

But yes, having two separate dedicated/specialised methods with long-winded names like this can be improved! Maybe a companion to `index_of` like `index_of_not`, adding a new "strategy" param to both that could default to "first" but also allow "last"? Or just a boolean "last" param that defaults to False. Would map conceptually to `is_null` and `is_not_null`, but be more generic 🤔 

Part of the problem for making the API clean/clear is that there is no single token we can pass in that just means "not null" (like... `lit(None).not()`, hah), and setting up boolean masks can (sometimes) be clunky. Anyway, I'll think about the comments and see what works and looks clean (an "ignore_nulls" param for `first`/`last` would be a good related addition - can look at that too) 👍

In the meantime have broken out the performance optimisations into a separate PR so that this one can be more API focused and not hold-up the speedups.

body:
So, my method does work, but with `is_in_list` it wouldn't be super easy to implement without a decent amount of bloat. For the record, suppose we have d_ns = datetime(ns)` and `d_us = datetime(us)` and we want `d_ns.is_in(d_us)`:

1. Record `d_ns % 1_000 != 0`. These values *cannot* be in `d_us` because they contain higher precision data than `d_us` can hold.
2. Record `d_ns.is_null()`, then downcast `d_ns` to `d_ns(us)`.
3. Compare `d_ns(us).is_null()`. The new null values are values were nullified by the cast, and therefore *cannot* be in `d_us`.
4. The bitwise `or` of (1) and (3) are a mask indicating which values *must* be False.
5. Return `d_ns(us).is_in(d_us) & !mask`.

...but in practice, with Lists and what not, this would basically duplicate all of the existing boilerplate code. If you have a good dynamic literal solution that sounds like it might be better I'm all ears, but I do question how python datetime literals are supposed to interact with nanosecond data, or how `is_in()` for two different time unit series is supposed to be handled. The above seems like a good correct solution that avoids upcasts.

body:
@coastalwhite I admit that the current warning/error system feels off to me, as I would bet that the most common usage of `is_in` is when an explicit list of potential values is provided in a python list. If the integer dtypes don't quite match and require upcasting, then having strict dtype matching would preclude users from being able to call e.g. `pl.col("uint8").is_in([1, 2, 3])` without explicitly casting the argument list, which a syntactic nightmare.

The same issue applies here for python datetimes. Aside from the performance cost, I don't see the issue in a lossless upcast of the LHS, as it preserves all information--and if we're dealing with a case where the LHS value is invalidated due to being outside the new upcasted range, then it's *impossible* for the `is_in` call to evaluate to True on that element, it *must* be False.

Using [max datetime values](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/21910#issuecomment-2749523049) as reference:

```python
s_milli = pl.Series([datetime(2025, 1, 1), datetime(9999, 1, 1)], dtype=pl.Datetime("ms"))
s_nano = pl.Series([datetime(2025, 1, 1)], dtype=pl.Datetime("ns"))
s_milli.is_in(s_nano)
# Error: 'is_in' cannot check for Nanoseconds precision values in Milliseconds Datetime data
```
Upcasting the LHS in this case would  result in two elements: [2025-01-01, \<out of bounds\>]. We *know* that the out of bounds value is not in the RHS. This *must always* be the case. Surely we can keep a path for datetimes where we simply track the invalidated values after the upcast? This is easy by comparing the original null mask to the casted null mask.
pr_title: fix: Ensure time unit upcast for temporal `is_in`

body:
It seems to me that `.show_graph()` becomes quite complicated by returning various output types depending on the arguments. It's also not very clear from the outside how those arguments interact. For example if I read 
```
.show_graph(show=True, raw_output_format="mermaid", output_path="foobar")
```
then it's not clear to me what I should expect (the current behavior would be to ignore `show` and `output_path`).

Since `to_dot()` and `to_mermaid()` already exist on the Rust side, wouldn't it be better to have the following function signatures in Python?

```
def to_dot(
    self,
    *,
    [ optimization args ]
) -> str

def to_mermaid(
    self,
    *,
    [ optimization args ]
) -> str

def show_graph(
    self,
    *,
    format = "graphviz",
    output_path = None,
    [ optimization args ]
) -> None
```
pr_title: feat: Add mermaid output to `show_graph`

body:
@etiennebacher thanks for these comments. Initially, I assumed that anyone needing to output a file would use Graphviz, but you're correct that it is confusing if `output_path` is silently ignored. It's also possible to generate the output files with a subprocess call in the same way that it is done for graphviz. I've updated the PR to support output file generation with both graphviz and mermaid. 

I have also incorporated @mcrumiller's suggestion, and the mermaid graph now uses monospace font when showing or outputting. 

My goal with this PR was to add mermaid support without changing the existing API. I have no issue with dedicated functions to access the dot or mermaid raw outputs, but to maintain backwards compatibility we would need to keep logic in `show_graph`, so it's not clear if that would be worth it.

One small change to note: previously, calls to `show_graph` with an output path or `show=True` raised an error if Graphviz wasn't installed. With this PR, in a notebook, a Mermaid graph is displayed without error, and if `mmdc` is installed, an output file is generated. I believe this is an improvement but wanted to flag it for clarity.

body:
A few issues -

Implementation-wise, it's better to write loops that directly gather the indices per-row, rather than the current 2-pass approach of constructing gather indices and then dispatching to gather.

This does seem to require a refactor of the existing logic (that gathers only a single value per row). I'd recommend using a similar code structure to the `horizontal_flatten` code in polars-compute

API-wise, `arr.gather(indices)` should follow the semantics of `arr.eval`, where -
* The `indices` parameter, as well as the return value from `arr.gather`, must be of an `Array` dtype by default
  * We'd ideally coerce literal types from `List` to `Array` in type coercion so that users can write e.g. `arr.gather([0,1,2])` instead of `arr.gather(pl.lit([0,1,2], dtype=pl.Array(pl.UInt32,3)))`
* After the above is supported, we could potentially add an `as_list: bool = False` parameter, similar to the one on `arr.eval`, to support gathering from Array->List

> Thanks! However, a hardcoded list isn't really a robust solution, and adds ongoing maintenance (if a new driver comes out we'd have to known about it somehow, update the list, and then push out a whole new release to pick up that support).
> 
> Is there no way to use the ADBC driver manager to confirm/discover drivers installed via `dbc` instead, if the module isn't found/available via a standard import? Then we would have automatic discovery as new drivers are made available.

ADBC seems to hide a lot of stuff behind driver manager's dbapi and packed into c extension. 
[Related Issue at adbc](https://github.com/apache/arrow-adbc/issues/2828) 
[Related closed pr](https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/24622) 
I refactored this portion of the code, the geist is if we are able to get a adbc `dbapi.Connection()`, then we already have a driver available and loaded, since a connection is either made through 
```
from adbc_driver_DRIVER_NAME import dbapi
dbapi.connect(uri = URI, ...)
```
or
```
from adbc_driver_manager import dbapi
dbapi.connect(driver = DRIVER_NAME, db_kwargs = ...)
```

body:
This has always been a thing in the back of my mind where it's undefined how this works. I'd assume that however it is, it should match the behaviour of `pl.DataFrame(...)` construction (see https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/25823/files). 

I'd propose the following, which feels aligned with the super messed-up way Python (and type checkers) think that ints and floats are "close enough to the same thing". For example, `assert 1 == 1.0` is True, Pyright doesn't warn about `-> float`-typed function returning an int, etc.

### Proposal

* A python int can be implicitly cast to any type of return_dtype int (lossless operation). Int overflows should raise an Exception.
* A python float can be implicitly cast to any type of return_dtype float (lossless operation). 
* A python int can be implicitly cast to any type of return_dtype float (lossless operation). 
* A python float CANNOT be implicitly cast to any type of return_dtype int (lossy operation).

Sorry for the delay. I had another look, and I think it's trying to shove too much into one function. I think there's three main use-cases:

1. Starting at some (date)time, repeatedly emit it and add increment until some endpoint is reached. This is covered currently by `pl.datetime_range` and `pl.date_range`.

2. Given some `start, end` pair, generate `n` samples within this (date)time range. This is covered by `pl.linear_space`.

3. Given some starting or stopping (date)time and an increment, generate exactly `n` outputs. This is currently not exactly covered.

Currently this PR is trying to put all three use-cases into one function, and that really complicates things, both for users and for the implementation in the back-end.

@mcrumiller Would it be possible for you to extract from this PR just the general improvements to the current `linear_space` / `date(time)_range` implementations, and write a proposal/do some brainstorming for a dedicated function for use-case number 3? Or correct me if I missed something?

body:
In all cases, the first value is the `start` and the last value is the `end`, the values move in the direction of the interval. So in your cases:

> If I do start as 1 Jan with interval='-1d' and num_samples=4, will it go 1 Jan, 31 Dec, 30 Dec, 29 Dec?

`[Jan 1, Dec 31, Dec 30, Dec 29]`. You specified the start (first value) to be Jan 1, and the interval between values is +1 days.

> What if I do end as 1 Jan with interval='1d' and num_samples=4?

`[Dec 29, Dec 30, Dec 31, Jan 1]`. You specified the end (last value) to be Jan 1, and the interval between values is +1 day.

What if I do end as 1 Jan with interval='-1d' and num_samples=4?

`[Jan 4, Jan 3, Jan 2, Jan 1]`. You specified the end (last value) to be Jan 1, and the interval between values is -1 days.

I agree that it is a slight headache here, but the logic is consistent. I was sure to test all of these cases, which is why the test suite is so large.

body:
While I appreciate this change (and it is arguably the correct behaviour), I believe that it is breaking longstanding behaviour.

For example, the code below currently writes a table to the database, but under these changes, would no longer do so.
It forces the user to change `connect(uri)` to `connect(uri, autocommit=True)` or to add `conn.commit()` before exiting the context manager - that being the breaking change.

```python
from adbc_driver_postgresql.dbapi import connect
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": 1})
uri = "postgresql://postgres:postgres@localhost:5433"
# autocommit defaults to False in `connect()`
with connect(uri) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:
    df.write_database("public.my_table", conn)
```


I appreciate that by default, the ADBC connections have `autocommit` off (for PEP 249 compliance) ([Source](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/current/python/api/adbc_driver_manager.html#adbc_driver_manager.AdbcConnection.set_autocommit:~:text=initialize%20the%20connection.-,autocommit,default.%20A%20warning%20will%20be%20emitted%20if%20it%20cannot%20be%20disabled.,-adbc_driver_manager.dbapi.)), but at the moment Polars is still committing the user's behalf.

Perhaps there is a way to introduce this additional flexibility without being a breaking change. A way to specify that you do not want Polars to commit on your behalf.
pr_title: fix(python): Enable manual commits for `write_database` with the ADBC engine

body:
Ok, I understand that this would be a breaking change. My opinion is that having `autocommit=False` and then polars still doing the `conn.commit()` on the users behalf undermines somewhat the purpose of the `autocommit=False` default of PEP249 because, for the user, the commit happens automatically anyway.  
However, perhaps compliance with PEP 249 can be maintained with the following suggestion? Introduce a boolean [pl.Config option](https://docs.pola.rs/api/python/stable/reference/config.html#) to give the possibility to turn off the `conn.commit()` in `frame.py` I proposed, e.g. something like `Config.set_autocommit` for ADBC. If other db engines have the same issue, the pl.Config option could also be designed for the other engines.

body:
Adding a real-world case to back up this PR, since the thread stalled on the breaking-change concern.

We maintain an internal library that wraps `write_database` for a PostgreSQL-based data warehouse. The core design requirement is that the **caller owns the transaction boundary** — our library accepts an optional external connection and commits only when it created the connection itself:

```python
owns_conn = conn is None
# ...
with ctx as effective_conn:
    for batch in all_batches:
        batch.write_database(
            table_name, effective_conn,
            if_table_exists="append",
            engine="adbc"
        )

    if owns_conn:
        effective_conn.commit()
    # caller-owned connections: caller commits externally
```

With current polars this pattern is broken: every `write_database` call silently commits mid-batch regardless of who owns the connection, making atomic multi-batch writes impossible when `conn` is caller-supplied. Our current workaround is applying this patch manually to polars at Docker build time. We would very much prefer a way to optin to the behaviour of this PR.

Hiding the change behind an opt-in flag would resolve both the original issue and the breaking change — existing behaviour is preserved by default, and library authors who need transaction control can set the flag. Something like:

```python
                    mode=mode,
                    **(engine_options or {}),
                )
                if not POLARS_ADBC_NO_AUTOCOMMIT:  # env-var/global config opt-in
                    conn.commit()
            return n_rows
        elif engine == "sqlalchemy":
```

The mechanism behind the flag implementation is debatable. The goal would be to have the feature available with the least amount of friction, with the bonus of having a migration/deprecation path in the future.

> an argument to disable upcasting the data

Calling `diff` on an unsigned integer dtype without a cast to signed does not really make sense. If your data is not ascending sorted, the diff will produce negatives, so a cast is required . Right now, every integer type is already upcast to the next-highest signed version (`u8 → i16`, `u16 → i32`, `u32 → i64`). For `u64` there was no upcast.

body:
Rebased onto current `main` (the branch had drifted 603 commits behind); no conflicts, and the change is unchanged.

Restating the bug, since this has been open a while. When `encoding` is not `utf8`/`utf8-lossy`, `prepare_file_arg` reads the file in Python and re-encodes it to UTF-8. It opens the file in text mode without `newline=`, so Python's universal-newline translation rewrites the bytes before the CSV parser ever sees them:

```python
>>> data = 'a,b\r\n1,"x\r\ny"\r\n'          # CRLF file, embedded CR in a quoted field
>>> p.write_bytes(data.encode("latin-1"))

>>> p.open(encoding="latin-1").read().encode("utf8")
b'a,b\n1,"x\ny"\n'                          # CRLF collapsed to LF

>>> p.open(encoding="latin-1", newline="").read().encode("utf8")
b'a,b\r\n1,"x\r\ny"\r\n'                    # preserved
```

The second line is what the file actually contains. The first is what polars currently parses, so a `\r\n` inside a quoted field is silently corrupted, and the transcoded path disagrees with the UTF-8 path on the same input.

`newline=""` is the documented way to disable that translation and hand the bytes through untouched. The fix adds it at the two `Path(file).open(...)` sites in `prepare_file_arg`, and the added test covers the quoted-field case.

body:
@eitsupi 

Thanks for flagging #24559 - I had a look and there is overlap in motivation, but the approaches differ in an important way.

#24559 proposes removing the automatic conn.commit() entirely and setting `autocommit=True` on connections, which is a breaking change - existing users who rely on Polars committing on their behalf would need to update their code. That PR also has unresolved discussion around this concern.

This PR takes a backward-compatible, opt-in approach: the default remains `commit=True` (existing behavior is unchanged), and users who need transaction control explicitly pass `commit=False`. It also adds a UserWarning when `commit=False` is used on a connection that already has autocommit enabled, since the intent to defer the commit cannot be honored in that case.

Happy to defer to the maintainers on which approach is preferred, or to align with #24559 if that direction is chosen.

body:
Thank you, I have a comment to the following quote from https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/27500. Your first post here also says it "UserWarning — data will not be persisted".
> **Autocommit interactions**
> 
> When an ADBC connection has autocommit=True, each statement is committed by the driver immediately and commit=False cannot be honoured. A UserWarning is emitted in this case:
> 
> UserWarning: commit=False has no effect because the ADBC connection has autocommit
enabled (or the driver does not support transactions). Data will be committed automatically.

In my opinion, it would be clearer to raise an error than a UserWarning when `autocommit=True` and `commit=False` because think of the following situation.
Someone writes a code with `autocommit=True` in the ADBC connection and an `write_database` without specifying the `commit` parameter. Then later on, he specifies `commit=False` in `write_database` because he thinks that this allows to manage the transaction himself and he forgets to change `autocommit` to `False` or he doesn't even know that `autocommit=True` overrules `commit=False`. Then, for example, he executes this code in a notebook's code cell, which leads to data being unintentionally written to the database. Raising an error would prevent such a mistake.

And my second point is, I noticed the following parameter description:

> Note: when ``connection`` is a URI string, Polars opens and closes the
            connection internally; setting ``commit=False`` in that case means the
            data will not be persisted.

Maybe is there an opportunity to use `commit=False` when `connection` is an URI string? That would be very convinient.

body:
@nameexhaustion would love to hear your (or, fwiw, anyone's) feedback on this feature. Before looking at the actual code, it might be worth aligning on the Python API though.

Currently, I chose the callback args to provide a list of `SinkedFileInfo` objects that are structured as follows:

```python
class SinkedFilesCallbackArgs:
   files: list[SinkedFileInfo]


class SinkedFileInfo:
    path: str
    partition_keys: DataFrame # exactly one row
    num_rows: int
    file_size_bytes: int
    parquet: ParquetFileMetadata | None = None


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class ParquetFileMetadata:
    footer_size_bytes: int
    column_stats: list[ParquetColumnStats]


@dataclass(kw_only=True)
class ParquetColumnStats:
    field_id: int
    compressed_size_bytes: int
    null_count: int | None
    min_value: Any | None
    max_value: Any | None
```

---

I now thought about this a little more and one might also want to consider a dataframe-centric approach similar to how `TableStatistics` in `scan_parquet` is constructed. For example:

```python
class SinkedFilesCallbackArgs:
   # This is only the path names, keeping the previous naming
   paths: list[str]
   # One row per file, i.e. path
   partition_keys: DataFrame
   # One row per file, i.e. path
   statistics: DataFrame
```

where the statistics data frame has the following schema (mirroring the `TableStatistics` approach):

```
num_rows:            UInt64
file_size_bytes:     UInt64
footer_size_bytes:   UInt64
<column>_size_bytes: UInt64
<column>_min:        [dtype dependent on column] (nullable)
<column>_max:        [dtype dependent on column] (nullable)
<column>_null_count: UInt64 (nullable)
```

The "downside" of this is that we are losing some column stats, namely for nested types (e.g. list elements or struct fields) which _would_ theoretically be available. The upside is that we are getting rid of field IDs in the public API. Some nested types (e.g. struct fields) could also potentially be supported in the future.

body:
You're right — accepting a list where all values must match isn't useful. The limitation is that `.over()` packs multiple `order_by` columns into a struct and sorts with a single `SortOptions`, which only has one `descending: bool`. Supporting mixed per-column directions would require changing `over_with_options` to accept `SortMultipleOptions` and propagating that through `Expr::Over`, `AExpr::Over`, and the physical expression layer.

This PR at least unblocks the common case (`descending=[True, True]` or `[False, False]`) that previously crashed with a `TypeError`, and gives a clear error for the mixed case instead of the confusing cast error. But I understand if you'd rather wait for a proper per-column implementation — happy to close this if that's preferred.

body:
I still don't see the point of this very specific exception sorry. In general having very large values can result in NaNs depending on evaluation order. Consider the following six numbers:

```python
a = 1
b = -1
c = 1e308
d = -1e308
e = 1e308
f =  -1e308
```

Naturally, these six numbers sum to 0. But depending on the order you sum them in you could get wildly different answers:

```python
>>> (a + b) + (c + d) + (e + f)
0.0
>>> (c + a + d) + (e + f) + b
-1.0
>>> (c + b + d) + (e + f) + a
1.0
>>> (c + e) + (d + f) + (a + b)
nan
>>> ((c + e) + d) + (f + a + b)
inf
>>> ((d + f) + c) + (e + a + b)
-inf
```

This is just how floats work. Either something needs to be fully robust or just accept this. Checking for very specific cases then re-trying hoping it gets better with a different order isn't particularly useful in my opinion.

> Actually, isn't `nt1=pl.ntile(2).over(order_by="value")` just `pl.col.value.qcut(2)`? 

Unfortunately not; there **is** overlap, but only when the partition height divides evenly by `n` and all the ordering values are distinct -- otherwise they won't tie-out:
```python
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({"value": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]})

df.with_columns(
    # ntile and qcut match here...
    ntile_3=pl.ntile(3).over(order_by="value"),
    qcut_3=pl.col("value").qcut(3, labels=["1","2","3"]),
    
    # ...but don't match here
    ntile_4=pl.ntile(4).over(order_by="value"),
    qcut_4=pl.col("value").qcut(4, labels=["1","2","3","4"]),
)
# shape: (6, 5)
# ┌───────┬─────────┬────────┬─────────┬────────┐
# │ value ┆ ntile_3 ┆ qcut_3 ┆ ntile_4 ┆ qcut_4 │
# │ ---   ┆ ---     ┆ ---    ┆ ---     ┆ ---    │
# │ i64   ┆ u32     ┆ cat    ┆ u32     ┆ cat    │
# ╞═══════╪═════════╪════════╪═════════╪════════╡
# │ 10    ┆ 1       ┆ 1      ┆ 1       ┆ 1      │
# │ 20    ┆ 1       ┆ 1      ┆ 1       ┆ 1      │
# │ 30    ┆ 2       ┆ 2      ┆ 2       ┆ 2      │
# │ 40    ┆ 2       ┆ 2      ┆ 2       ┆ 3      │  <- differs
# │ 50    ┆ 3       ┆ 3      ┆ 3       ┆ 4      │  <- differs
# │ 60    ┆ 3       ┆ 3      ┆ 4       ┆ 4      │  <- differs

> > Unfortunately not; there is overlap, but only when the partition height divides evenly by n and all the ordering values are distinct -- otherwise they won't tie-out:
> 
> I'm not sure if the highlighted difference is relevant in practice. It still satisfies the original definition "Splits an ordered dataset into a specified number of roughly equal groups (that cannot differ in size by more than 1),", even if the exact group which is 1 larger is a bit different.

`ntile` additionally specifies that if the number of tiles doesn't evenly divide the total size then the remainder is assigned to the "lower" tiles (as defined by the order-by clause).

So supposing you have $N$ values, and $q$ tiles. Then tile $i$ has 

$$
\left\lfloor\frac{N}{q}\right\rfloor + \begin{cases} 1, & i < (N \mod q) \\\\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
$$

rows.

body:
Checking in on this one, it's been open about three weeks without a review.

Worth flagging the impact since it produces wrong results silently rather than being cosmetic. `dt.date()` and `dt.truncate()` copy the input's sorted flag onto their output, but neither is monotonic for tz-aware input. Once the flag is wrongly set to `SORTED_ASC`, `.sort()` turns into a no-op, `min()` can return something that isn't the minimum, and `join_asof` / `group_by_dynamic` quietly consume the wrong ordering. Both repros are in #28560.

On verification: I swept all 598 zones in the tz database over hourly data from 2005 to 2016 for `dt.date()` and `dt.truncate()` with `1h`, `30m` and `1d` windows, and nothing claims `SORTED_ASC` while actually being unsorted. Positive controls confirm tz-naive and UTC input still keep the flag, including `1mo` and `1y` windows and `Date` input, so this isn't just dropping sortedness across the board.

If it's easier to review as two separate PRs I can split the `dt.date()` and `dt.truncate()` halves apart.
pr_title: fix: Don't preserve sorted flag through non-monotonic `dt.date()`/`dt.truncate()`

Addressed the Codecov patch-coverage flag by adding unit tests for `split_to_morsels`.

**On the coverage report itself**

The diff moves a function without touching it, which Codecov counts as 26 new lines and
re-evaluates from scratch. The totals line in its own report confirms nothing was added:

```
Lines   262968   262968       0
```

I diffed the relocated body against `HEAD~1` - 21 lines, byte-identical, no logic change.
The one uncovered line was the `else { 1 }` arm, and it was equally uncovered at the old
location: `parquet/init.rs` only ever had `test_filtered_range`, never a test for
`split_to_morsels`. So this is a pre-existing gap that the move made visible rather than a
regression.

**Tests added**

Rather than just point that out, the gap is now closed - four cases covering each branch:

| test | what it pins |
| --- | --- |
| `stays_whole_below_the_split_threshold` | the `else { 1 }` arm (height <= 1.5x ideal), the previously uncovered line |
| `splits_above_the_threshold` | multi-morsel path, and that row count is conserved |
| `last_morsel_respects_pipeline_count` | `n_morsels.max(last_morsel_pipelines)` spreading a small frame across pipelines |
| `empty_frame_yields_nothing` | the `filter(height > 0)` guard on an empty frame |

- `cargo test -p polars-stream --features parquet morsel_split` - 4 passed, 0 failed.

body:
Thanks, this is a solid start. A few design directions worth considering before diving into the code.

### 1. Run min/max first, then probe blooms on the survivors

min/max is free (already in the footer) and blooms cost range reads, so running min/max first and probing blooms only on the survivors gets the same result with far less IO. Sequencing the filters this way also leaves a natural place for page-index and dictionary pruning to slot in later as additional stages.

### 2. Fetch the minimum per probe

- **One block instead of the whole filter.** A value's hash addresses a single 32-byte block, and `is_in_set` reads exactly that, so reading the header for `num_bytes` and then fetching only the addressed block(s) (one per value for `is_in`) would save a lot of IO on high-cardinality columns. Adaptive is the sweet spot: read small filters whole, fetch single blocks for large ones.
- **Concurrent, coalesced reads.** Issuing the per-row-group reads concurrently and coalescing adjacent ranges would speed this up considerably on high-latency storage.
- **Hoist the invariant work.** Hash each literal once rather than per row group, and reuse `collect_bloom_preds` rather than computing it twice per file.

These mainly matter on object storage, so they're easy to miss against a local-NVMe benchmark.

### 3. Cost-based gating

Putting bloom probing behind a cost-based decision (row-group count, filter size, selectivity) would keep it a win across workloads, and the `is_in` threshold is a nice start in that direction. The two knobs (`POLARS_NO_BLOOM_FILTER_PRUNE`, `POLARS_BLOOM_IN_FILTER_THRESHOLD`) would also fit well as typed getters in `polars-config` alongside `prune_parquet_metadata`, which gives consistent parsing, caching, and reload in one place rather than ad-hoc `std::env::var` reads.

### 4. Considering dictionary pruning

For a fully dictionary-encoded chunk the dictionary is an exact membership set (no false positives), so it's strictly stronger than a probabilistic bloom. We don't have dict-based row-group skipping yet, so a short comment capturing the intended design would help for now: prefer dictionary pruning on dict-encoded chunks, falling back to the bloom if one is present. Since probing the dictionary means decoding it and building a lookup set (cost scales with dictionary size), dictionary pruning should be cost-based too, enabled when the dictionary is small.

### Correctness

Parquet has no integer type below `INT32`, so `Int8/16` and `UInt8/16` columns are stored as `INT32` and the writer hashes 4 bytes. For those types `scalar.rs` currently hashes the native 1 to 2 bytes, so the probe hash won't match the stored one and matching row groups can be skipped. Widening the value to its physical type before hashing resolves it (routing through the existing `hash_native` / `hash_byte` keeps the probe and writer in sync), and an `Int8`/`Int16` test with a present value would lock it in.

body:
Took this over from @waamm. Added on top:

1. Probe only when we hash the exact bytes the writer hashed: floats (signed zero), bools, `Time` (ns vs TIME(MICROS)) and cast projections are excluded. Each could report a present value as absent and silently drop rows.
2. Malformed filter headers no longer panic (regression test from raw bytes).
3. Bloom IO moved to the tokio runtime; it panicked on real cloud sources before.
4. One env var: `POLARS_BLOOM_FILTER_PRUNE` = `off` (default), `auto` (prune local sources with block reads, skip cloud), `whole` / `blocks` (force pruning on any source with either read strategy).
5. Rust unit tests for the header guard and env var parsing; the Python tests need pyarrow >= 24 for `bloom_filter_options` and skip on older.

Benchmark: ClickBench q19 with bloom filters on `hits` (UserID, 100M rows, scattered so min/max prunes nothing). Identical rows in every configuration.

| `POLARS_BLOOM_FILTER_PRUNE` | local SSD (warm) | simulated S3 (30 ms RTT) | S3 bytes read |
|---|---|---|---|
| `off` | 8.6 ms | 10.3 s | 173.2 MB |
| `auto` | 1.2 ms (7x) | 10.3 s (no probing) | 173.2 MB |
| `blocks` | 1.2 ms (7x) | 43 s | 1.9 MB (1.1%) |
| `whole` | 2.5 ms | 22 s | 25.9 MB (15%) |

`blocks` is byte optimal and wins locally; `whole` halves cloud round trips but serial per row group probing still loses to no pruning at 30 ms RTT, hence `auto` skips cloud and the default stays off. Concurrent probe fetching is the follow up that should flip cloud to a win; the benchmark harness is its acceptance test.

I used Claude to implement this. I reviewed the code myself.

Thanks for pointing this out. I checked the nearby read functions:

- `read_json` and `read_ndjson` do not expose a `use_pyarrow` parameter, and both pass `schema`/`schema_overrides` through their native Polars read paths.
- `read_parquet` does expose `use_pyarrow`, but it already rejects `schema` together with `use_pyarrow=True` by raising `ValueError("`schema` cannot be used with `use_pyarrow=True`")`.
- `read_ipc` and `read_ipc_stream` expose `use_pyarrow`, but they do not expose a `schema` parameter, so there is no equivalent `schema`/`use_pyarrow` interaction there.

So this appears specific to `read_csv`, where the PyArrow CSV parser path can be selected while the `schema` parameter is still accepted at the API level.
pr_title: docs(python): Clarify read_csv use_pyarrow behavior

body:
If the behavior for `pl.read_parquet` is that we return an error, I think that—for the sake of consistency—we should move towards that behavior for `read_csv` too in the future. However, that would add a breaking change.

I think that for now the actual issue is not really the docstring, but that polars discards the `schema` parameter. As such, it does not adhere to the claim made in `use_pyarrow`:

```
    use_pyarrow
        Try to use pyarrow's native CSV parser. This will always
        parse dates, even if `try_parse_dates=False`.
        This is not always possible. The set of arguments given to
        this function determines if it is possible to use pyarrow's
        native parser. Note that pyarrow and polars may have a
        different strategy regarding type inference.
```

When the `schema` parameter is set, then we actually cannot use pyarrow, so we should fall back to using the polars parser.

As such I think we should not update the docs here, but add the `schema` parameter to the check:

```
    if (
        use_pyarrow
        and schema is None # <- here
        and schema_overrides is None
        and n_rows is None
        and n_threads is None
        and not low_memory
        and null_values is None
    ):
```

Still, I suspect that part of the confusion for https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/issues/19886 is that for `read_csv`, the `use_pyarrow` parameter is more like a hint, and the user does not get to know when it is dropped. I think that in these cases a warning should be emitted (until we can bump to a new major version, in which I think it should become an error).

Cc @ritchie46, @orlp. Do you have any opinions on this?

     column.rs:127 assumes each current group corresponds to an outer row. Windows create additional subgroups, breaking that mapping:

     df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [[1, 2], []], "y": [10, 20]})
     df.select(
         pl.col("x").list.eval(
             (pl.element().sum() + pl.col("y")).over(pl.element())
         )
     )

     Both engines return [[11, 22], []]; expected [[11, 12], []]. Other subgroup counts trigger an assertion panic.

  2. [P2] Nested evaluations panic over null outer arrays or masked lists.
     eval.rs:674 sizes gather using the sum of valid group lengths, but group offsets still include masked children. With x = [[[1], [2]], None, [[3],
     [4]]] typed as Array(List(Int64), 2), evaluating x.arr.eval(pl.element().list.eval(pl.element() + pl.col("y"))) panics: range end index 6 out of
     range for slice of length 4. The mapping must cover the complete flattened index space.

  3. [P2] Broadcast literals lose their column dependencies in streaming.
     expr_to_ir.rs:518 now permits these references, but streaming’s input-independence analysis still examines only eval’s input:

     pl.LazyFrame({"y": [10, 20]}).select(
         pl.lit([1, 2]).list.eval(pl.element() + pl.col("y"))
     ).collect(engine="streaming")

     This raises ColumnNotFoundError for y; in-memory execution succeeds. Streaming planning must retain evaluation-column dependencies.

  4. [P2] Null literals skip broadcasting and return the wrong height.
     Broadcasting at eval.rs:208 happens after the all-null early return. Selecting pl.lit(None, dtype=pl.List(pl.Int64)).list.eval(pl.element() +
     pl.col("y")) against three rows returns one null row instead of three. This affects all four list/array eval/agg variants.


```

body:
I reviewed this in depth, including building it locally and running the reproduction cases directly, not just reading the diff. One thing changes what should happen with this PR before merge, so I'll lead with that.

## The bug this fixes may already be gone on main, through an unrelated commit

This branch is based on a commit from August 4th. On August 14th, `bf439efa2d` ("chore: Use canonical expression IDs in CSEE", #28786) landed and replaced the `Identifier`/`IdentifierMap` subexpression tracking this PR patches with a different `NodeRole`/`classify`/`CanonicalExprMap` scheme. That's an unrelated refactor, not a fix for #28653.

I built polars from a branch descending from that commit (current main) without this PR's patch and ran:

```python
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"g": [1, 1, 2]})
lit = pl.lit(-1.5).abs()
q = lf.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg(a=lit, b=lit)
q.collect()
```

Result: `a=[1.5, 1.5], b=[1.5, 1.5]`, matching the unoptimized baseline. Not the `list[f64]` bug from the issue. I also ran this PR's own new test, the mixed scalar plus column expression variant posted in the issue thread, and a three way shared scalar case. All four came back correct on unpatched current main.

I don't know the exact mechanism responsible. `classify()` on current main still marks `lit(-1.5).abs()` as a `Candidate` in group by mode, and `q.explain()` shows the same shape the bug report describes: a hoist into `WITH_COLUMNS` followed by `.implode()` per group. Yet the result comes out scalar and correct. Something downstream now handles it properly, most likely as a side effect of the CSEE rewrite. Worth noting #28653 is still open and this is the only PR linked to it, so nobody has flagged the bug as independently resolved.

Practically: this patch targets code that no longer exists on main. Before merging, it needs a rebase, and the two new tests should be run against current main with the code change reverted to see if they already pass without it. If they do, the fix itself is moot, but the tests are still worth keeping as a permanent regression guard for #28653 since the issue remains open.

## On the patch itself, assuming its target mechanism still applies somewhere

I traced `find_cse` and confirmed that in the `IR::GroupBy` arm, `aggs.cse_exprs()` is the complete set of subexpressions shared anywhere in that group_by node, not one candidate at a time. So the `all_column_height` check is all or nothing per group_by call: if a single scalar height candidate is present, hoisting is skipped for every other candidate too, even ones that are genuinely safe to share.

Concretely, sharing `pl.col("x") * 2` across `.sum()` and `.mean()` in the same `.agg()` call as a `lit(...).abs()` output would silently lose that valid sharing. No wrong result, just a missed optimization with no test coverage either way, since none of the current cases in `test_cse.py` mix a scalar height candidate with a column height one in the same group_by.

## Verdict

Hold. This is a correct, well targeted fix for the code it was written against, but that code has moved and the specific bug does not currently reproduce on main independent of this patch. Needs a rebase and reverification before merge, and the mixed case test gap is worth closing regardless of how the primary question resolves.
pr_title: fix: Prevent CSE from sharing scalar aggs in group_by()

body:
Thanks for the thorough review.

On whether the bug still reproduces: confirmed it does, on the actual released Polars 1.44.1, but not on the current main branch.

On the granularity issue, you're right too, and I was able to reproduce it concretely against my patched branch:

```python
lf = pl.LazyFrame({"g": [1, 1, 2], "x": [10, 20, 30]})
q = lf.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg(
    a=pl.lit(-1.5).abs(), b=pl.lit(-1.5).abs(),
    c=(pl.col("x") * 2).sum(), d=(pl.col("x") * 2).mean(),
)
```

Results are correct, but:

```
AGGREGATE[maintain_order: true]
  [dyn float: -1.5.abs().alias("a"), dyn float: -1.5.abs().alias("b"), (col("x") * 2).sum().alias("c"), (col("x") * 2).mean().alias("d")] BY [col("g")]
  FROM
  DF ["g", "x"]; PROJECT */2 COLUMNS
```

No `WITH_COLUMNS`. `col("x") * 2` gets computed twice instead of shared, because my `all_column_height` check blocks the whole node's hoist when any candidate is non-scalar-height. Thanks for pointing it out.

I also ran this same mixed case against unpatched current `main`, and it's fine there too: `col("x") * 2` gets correctly hoisted alongside the scalar, same results.

**Verdict:** broken in the latest release (1.44.1), fixed on current `main`, likely a side effect of #28786's `CanonicalExprMap` rewrite, though I haven't pinned the exact commit responsible.

Given that, I'd suggest closing this PR as moot, but I'll add two regression tests (scalar-only and mixed scalar+column) rebased onto current `main`, since #28653 stays open and nothing currently guards against a regression on either case. Let me know if that's the right call or if you'd prefer something else.

body:
That being said, after looking into it some more, it should still be a fix for the Spearman method. The Spearman method never feeds raw values into the kernel like Pearson does, it gives ranks. The ranks are always integers or half integers, so every step in the kernel should be exact and no rounding should occur. For example:

```text
sum         = 123.0 × 117 = 14391.0     exact (integer arithmetic under 2^53)
mean_x      = 14391.0 / 117 = 123.0     exact (true answer is representable)
xi - mean_x = 0.0                       exact
dp_xx       = 0.0                       exact
finalize    → dp_xx * dp_yy > 0.0 is false → NaN
```

So the `NaN` isn't a boundary result because `dp_xx` is a true zero. The only step that could round, in the case of the MRE, was `1 / 117` because `1/ 117` isn't representable, which would add noise downstream. Replacing it with a direct division removes the one inexact operation, which is why this fix works for Spearman. 

For Pearson, the raw values go straight into the kernel. If the constant is representable, the path is exact just like Spearman's. If it isn't, the stored values are inexact before any math runs, so the sum rounds and no exact answer is possible.

body:
@ritchie46 Just ran a diagnostic using Fable and:

The sources and the in-memory engine are all 1 chunk; the streaming engine emits ~250 chunks for `join1` and 5,000 for `join2` under `POLARS_IDEAL_MORSEL_SIZE=4`, so this is morsel-sized output not being coalesced, which I take to be by design for that config. The slow part is `assert_frame_equal(check_row_order=False)` on that layout (~50s per call, ~0.1s after rechunk). So for the fix, we can keep the rechunk in the helper, or look at making the unordered comparison robust to chunked input instead. Side note: 5,000 chunks is one per wide row rather than one per morsel; not sure if that's expected.

pr_title: test: Rechunk before comparison in join pushthrough tests

body:
The chunk count for `join1` follows the morsel size: 1,000 fact rows / 4 per morsel ≈ 250 chunks, and that's what comes out (251).

For `join2` I'd expect the same pattern. Probing with `join1` (1,002 rows) would be ~250 morsels of 4, each row matching 100 `wide` rows → ~250 chunks of ~400 rows. Probing with `wide` (5,000 rows) would be ~1,250 morsels → ~1,250 chunks of ~80 rows.

Instead it comes out as 5,000 chunks of ~20 rows. That's one chunk per `wide` row (each `wide` row matches ~20 fact rows), i.e. the output is split 4× finer than the morsel size would suggest. Might be deliberate for expanding joins, but just flagging it in case it isn't.

body: @lorentzenchr the key distinctions between intervals/quantiles vs ranks is that the former do not split equivalent (equal) values across bins. If your data is skewed, quantile binning will therefore give imbalanced bins, and you might want to consider binning by ranks. For example, `bin_ranks` will split `[1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]` into as many bins as you would like, whereas `bin_quantiles` will keep all the 1s together.

codex: 

```
 - [P1] try_append silently replaces distinct values — scalar.rs lines 218–223

    AnyValue::PartialEq expresses analytical equality, not representational identity. Consequently, vstack can discard the right-hand value:
      - 0.0 followed by -0.0 becomes all positive zero, as the new test explicitly demonstrates.
      - _AlwaysEqual(1) followed by _AlwaysEqual(2) becomes two copies of the first object, losing i == 2.
      - Object appends now unexpectedly invoke arbitrary Python __eq__ code.

    Equality-based operations such as unique may canonicalize values, but concatenation should preserve them. The fast path should require representation-preserving
    identity, or fall back for floats, objects, and affected nested values.

```

body:
codex:

```
• Request changes — I found two correctness issues in PR #29147.

  1. [P1] Preserve logical nested dtypes before row-format sorting

     The new arg_sort call receives columns already converted with to_physical_repr() (sortby.rs L214-L245). This removes categorical mappings nested
     inside List, Struct, or Map columns. Row encoding consequently sorts physical category codes—in insertion order—instead of categorical values.

     Reproduced against the PR build:

     k = pl.Series("k", [["z"], ["a"], ["m"]], dtype=pl.List(pl.Categorical))
     df = pl.DataFrame({"k": k, "x": [0, 1, 2], "y": [0, 0, 0]})

     df.sort("k", "y")["x"].to_list()
     # [1, 2, 0]

     df.select(pl.col("x").sort_by("k", "y"))["x"].to_list()
     # [0, 1, 2]

     Map and Struct categoricals fail identically. The grouped path also physicalizes these columns (sortby.rs L310-L324) and returns the wrong order.
     Nested logical dtypes need to remain intact when passed to row encoding.

  2. [P2] Recursively validate Maps in the safe chunk constructor

     The new Series::from_chunk_and_dtype branch validates only when the outer dtype is Map, then calls the shallow MapChunked::try_from_storage (from.rs
     L48-L55). That method canonicalizes only the outer Map’s keys; nested Map children remain unchecked.

     A focused Rust test constructed Map(String, Map(String, Int64)) whose inner Map contained duplicate keys, passed its matching physical Arrow chunk to
     this safe function, and received Ok. The nested Map still contained two entries instead of the required canonicalized one. Maps inside List/Struct
     containers bypass this branch entirely.

     The safe constructor should recursively validate/canonicalize every Map reached through dtype.contains_map(), using logic equivalent to the existing
     recursive Series::canonicalize_maps.

  Validation performed on exact head 2a1dd385: isolated Python runtime built successfully; the complete modified Map and sort test modules passed (351
  passed, 5 deselected). Additional nested-Map UDF and null-ordering probes passed, while the categorical and constructor regressions above were
  independently reproduced. The main checkout remains clean.

```

> @nameexhaustion, should we communicate if we applied projection, limit, filters etc?

For filters, there is an `applied_filters: set[int]` that can be returned as part of `ResolvedLazyFrameProps`, to indicate which filters were applied by index.

For projection, we just always put a SimpleProjection on top, so no need to communicate.

For slice, because we only pass row-limit to the resolver, this also doesn't need indication of whether it was applied. But if we want to allow resolvers to receive full slices with potentially non-zero offsets, we do need a required return value of to signal whether the resolver applied the offset.

pr_title: fix: Error instead of segfault for `exp`/`log1p` on non-numeric dtypes

body:
@orlp 

Okay so `fn exp` in `log.rs` had a `match` statement for the `dtype` that determined what to do given the datatype of `s`. It properly handled integers and floats, but the catch-all was a recursive call:

```rust
_ => s.cast(&DataType::Float64).unwrap().exp(),
```

Which would cast `s` to `Float64` and then call `.exp()` again. In the case of a `Struct` datatype, each field in the `Struct` would be cast to `Float64`, but the outer container would still be a `Struct`, resulting in infinite recursion, which would grow the stack infinitely, and lead to stack overflow, eventually resulting in the OS killing the program. There is no `unsafe` code involved.

`polars_ensure!` prevents `Struct` from ever reaching the catch-all, so we prevent the eventual segfault. 

**Question for you:** Should we introduce `polars_bail!` in the catch-all so the recursion can't be re-introduced? If so, it would also potentially need to be introduced in `log` and `arctan2` as well since it also has a recursive catch-all.

body:
@coastalwhite I've ported the code, and now looking at addressing your comments.

* You brought up `pl.Series([1, 2, 3]).search_sorted([2, 3])` as a problem, but actually that is fine as far as _signature_ goes. Signature says `list[NonNestedLiteral] -> Series`, and that's what happens.
* `pl.Series([[1], [2], [3]).search_sorted([2, 3])` _does_ actually have the wrong signature, since it returns an integer index.

The obvious solution to get consistent signatures is to always interpret lists as literals. But that is _not backwards compatible_. `pl.Series([1, 2, 3]).search_sorted([2, 3])` will stop returning a `pl.Series` and instead raise an error.

## Some options

### Option 1. What's in the initial PR

1. Existing supported types are backwards compatible in that they take a list of values as if it were a `pl.Series` i.e. multi-search, and return a `pl.Series`.
2. Newly supported types (list and array) only accept `pl.Series` for multi-search, and a list is interpreted as a `pl.List` or `pl.Array`.

In Polars 2, where backwards compatibility could be dropped, one would then change the function so that lists are always interpreted as literals, and you always have to pass `pl.Series` for multi-search for all dtypes.

The problem with this is inconsistent type signatures. I do not see any way to fix this.

The benefit is fully backwards compatible, and nicer usage for `pl.List/pl.Array` dtypes.

This may be best demonstrated with some examples:

```python
# For non-nested types, both lists and Series result in Series (multi-search):
>>> pl.Series([17, 5]).search_sorted([17, 2, 5])
shape: (3,)
Series: '' [u32]
[
        2
        0
        0
]
>>> pl.Series([17, 5]).search_sorted(pl.Series([17, 2, 5]))
shape: (3,)
Series: '' [u32]
[
        2
        0
        0
]
>>> pl.Series([17, 5]).search_sorted(5)
0
# For a nested type, a list results in an int, but a Series results in a Series (multi-search):
>>> pl.Series([[17], [5]]).search_sorted([5])
0
>>> pl.Series([[17], [5]]).search_sorted(pl.Series([5]))
shape: (1,)
Series: '' [u32]
[
        0
]
```

### Option 2. Lists mean multi-search for `pl.List` and `pl.Array` dtypes

In this case `search_sorted([1, 2])` _always_ means multi-search. This is very annoying from a Python user perspective when using `pl.List/pl.Array` dtypes, since it's not DWIM.

### Option 3. ???

I get the impression you were suggesting something else in https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/pull/21266#pullrequestreview-2808343102 but I don't understand what, unfortunately.

@coastalwhite Can you maybe provide a Python example of both the signature, and what inputs/outputs you expect for primitive vs nested types given a list and given a Series?

body:
I think this should get a similar treatment to `.is_in` in such a way that we deprecate the usage of `pl.Series([1, 2, 3]).search_sorted([2, 3])` while also supporting nested types properly. For `.is_in()` this was done by changing the signature and adding an implicit `.implode()` in type coercion if the levels of nesting mismatched between the two arguments.

For `search_sorted`, we should not change the signature, but we should add an implicit `.explode()` in type coercion if the righthand side is 1 nesting level higher than the left side and throw a deprecation warning. Look at https://github.com/pola-rs/polars/blob/1a8a30b8f843c2cfa77bdf8874eb186f05c1d84e/crates/polars-plan/src/plans/conversion/type_coercion/is_in.rs#L33 for the implicit `.implode()` on `.is_in()`.

If you do this and remove the `list_as_series=True`, `pl.Series([1, 2, 3]).search_sorted([2, 3])` will still work but throw a deprecation warning. `pl.Series([1, 2, 3]).search_sorted(pl.Series([2, 3]))` will still work as before and you will be able to pass `pl.Series([[1], [2, 3]]).search_sorted([2, 3])` correctly.

body:
This was a second fix that was found by Claude while I was working on the fix outlined in the issue.

`year` is an `i32` while months is an `i64`. Converting `(months / 12)` to `i32` using `as i32` would result in truncation (and possibly returning a wrong date) if the resulting value didn't fit. 

Instead, we widen year to `i64`, which is lossless, then add `(months / 12)` to it. This is followed by doing `try_from` + `map_err` during the cast, so that it errors instead of silently truncating if the value exceeds the range.

This made sense to me. so I double checked it, implemented it, and added a test for this fix.

To test broader impact, I isolated generic construction path `DataFrameBuilder::reserve` → `SeriesBuilder::reserve` → `FixedSizeListArrayBuilder::reserve` I directly compare `reserve(additional)` with `reserve(additional * size)`. Each case processes 4,194,048 Int64 child values at widths 1, 8, 64, 768. Both modes reserve all outer rows first: single `extend` copies input once, while repeated `subslice_extend` copies approx 65,536 child values per call. Revisions: main `73dd5bea65`, PR `c25a47ca73`. Arrows in table mean main → PR. 100% means final child capacity equals required payload. | Mode | Width | Growth
reallocations | Final child capacity
/ required payload | | :--- | ---: | :---: | ---: | | single extend | 1 | 0 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | single extend | 8 | 1 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | single extend | 64 | 1 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | single extend | 768 | 1 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | repeated subslice_extend | 1 | 0 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | repeated subslice_extend | 8 | 3 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | repeated subslice_extend | 64 | 6 → 0 | 100.000% → 100.000% | | repeated subslice_extend | 768 | 8 → 0 | 199.231% → 100.000% | Corrected reservation eliminates every observed child-buffer growth reallocation for widths above 1. Most cases reach same capacity without intermediate growth, but **width 768 also reduces final capacity from 199.231% to 100% of required payload.**

body:
Thanks @coastalwhite — fair point on performance. Let me check what actually happens in the optimizer rather than argue.

The current code already routed list-of-columns through `F.struct(...)` (the else branch), so the struct path isn't new for the "several columns" case; the change extends it to also cover a single `pl.Expr`/selector (e.g. `pl.col("a", "b")`) and a single-element sequence, which previously fell into the fast `expr.n_unique()` path and only counted the first column.

If the optimizer doesn't fold `pl.struct(...)` here, the options are:
1. Keep the struct wrapper only when the subset expression/selector expands to more than one column (single-column expressions keep the fast path); or
2. Route through `self.lazy().unique(subset=subset)` semantics so the backend optimizes it the same way `unique()` already does.

I'll verify which the query optimizer does for `select(pl.struct(cols).n_unique())` — if it materializes structs via row-encoding, I'll go with option 1 and keep the fast path for the (common) single-column / plain-string case. Any preference on your side?
pr_title: fix(python): count all selected columns in DataFrame.n_unique

body:
@coastalwhite — good call, verified your concern: `pl.struct(...).n_unique()` was measurably slower than the direct path on a large frame, and the docstring size metric confirms the worry about row-encoding.

Reworked to your second option: `n_unique` now delegates to `self.unique(subset=subset)` and returns the resulting frame's `height`. That reuses the exact optimized path `unique()` already uses for multi-column expressions/selectors, is correct for every case in the issue (listed below), and keeps the fast path for single-column/string subsets via the backend.

Verified locally:
- `n_unique(pl.col("A","B"))` → 5 ✅
- `n_unique(cs.by_name("B","A"))` → 5 ✅
- `n_unique(pl.exclude("id"))` → 5 ✅
- `n_unique(["A","B"])` → 5 ✅
- `n_unique("A")` → 4 (single column, unchanged)
- empty frame → 0

Head `d93f726`, `py_compile` clean.
pr_title: fix(python): count all selected columns in DataFrame.n_unique

body:
@coastalwhite — reworking to the `unique(subset=...)` option surfaced a real problem I want to be honest about, so I've gone back to the `struct` wrapper.

Testing `self.unique(subset=...)` against the existing `n_unique` docstring case — `subset=[(pl.col("a") // 2), (pl.col("c") | (pl.col("b") >= 2))]` (expected 3) — **panicked in the backend**:

```
implementation error, cannot get ref Int64 from Int32
    at crates/polars-core/src/series/mod.rs
```

So delegating to `unique()` isn't a drop-in for `n_unique`: it can't handle the exact expression-subset case the method is documented to support. I verified the `struct` approach below gives the right answer for every case the method documents and the issue's reproducer — confirmed locally on the same frame the panic hit.

On the performance concern: the `struct` wrapper only applies when a `subset` is actually passed (the plain `n_unique()` with no subset still uses `F.struct(F.all())` as before), and it's the single correct path we have. If you know the optimizer does fold `pl.struct(cols).n_unique()` into a direct per-column path, happy to be shown otherwise.

Current head `1fdbfac`.
